candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: It leaves two jurisdictions a player can start in unplayable for the political half of the game, which is close to the refusal the range policy was written to abolish. It is also the status quo by accident rather than by decision, and the status quo currently reports DC as "refused" with no reason a player can read.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: The owner's three states for a rule are sourced law, generated-and-playable, and genuinely unknown. A territory and a federal district are the clearest case in the whole project of the third state: the endpoints the range would be measured between are state legislatures, and neither of these is one. This keeps the range honest by keeping it to the population it was measured from.
candidateAnswers.label: Treat both as genuinely unknown rather than generated
candidateAnswers.position: DC and Puerto Rico stay outside the range. Neither gets interpolated rules. Both are declared explicitly unsupported until somebody reads their actual law, and the surface says so in the game's own fail-soft voice rather than refusing silently.

candidateAnswers.argumentAgainst: It is two instruments to build, maintain and explain, for two jurisdictions, and each needs a named comparison group that somebody has to justify. It risks a bespoke rule path per jurisdiction, which is the thing the range exists to avoid.
candidateAnswers.argumentFor: They are not alike. DC has a Mayor and a Council and sends a Delegate; Puerto Rico has a bicameral legislature that does not resemble the state ones and sends a Resident Commissioner. Deciding them together is the same error as ranging them against states, one level up. This is also the only option that ends with both playable.
candidateAnswers.label: Each gets its own instrument
candidateAnswers.position: The two are decided separately, not as one class. DC is ranged or read against a comparison group it actually belongs to; Puerto Rico gets its own, drawn from a different group again or read from its real law. Neither inherits the state range.

notes: Current state, measured rather than assumed, because the question reads differently depending on the answer. Neither jurisdiction is currently governed by the national range, because the national range is not built: it is the owner's stated policy and has no implementation. DC today refuses candidacy for both chambers on a missing minimum age; Puerto Rico is not in the coverage report at all. That makes this a decision taken before the wrong rules exist rather than a correction after, which is the cheap end of it. It also names the live risk: the one generated-rule instrument that does exist is gated on a fifty-key state list, so a range built on the same gate would silently leave both jurisdictions permanently refused, and nothing would report that as a gap.

Filed deliberately as a design question rather than an engineering one. Whether a territory should be simulated by interpolation from states is a judgement about what the game is meant to cover, not something that can be settled by reading our own code.

The engineering half is separable and is ours: the code seats 52 jurisdictions and every document says 51. That is a correction to make regardless of how this is answered, and it does not wait on this.

How this was found is worth keeping. A lane's sweep walked a jurisdiction list somebody had typed from memory. The offered correction was to add DC by hand, which would have produced a list that looked complete and still had no Puerto Rico in it. Deriving the list from the code instead found the real count. The derived list was larger than the authored one, which is the second time tonight that has been true in this area.

Real law always overrides a generated range, per the owner's standing rule, so a decision to read either jurisdiction's actual law is compatible with everything already built and needs no new mechanism.

Two candidate answers are offered below so there is something to react to. Neither is recommended. This is a product judgement about what the game claims to cover, and it is the owner's call, not ours.
question: The game generates rules for an unresearched jurisdiction by drawing from the range the read states span, which varies state to state and stays stable per state across saves. That instrument was derived from states. Two of the jurisdictions the game actually seats are not states: the District of Columbia, governed by a Mayor and a Council and sending a Delegate rather than members, and Puerto Rico, whose legislature does not resemble the state legislatures the range was read from and which sends a Resident Commissioner. So: should either of them be governed by the national range at all? If not, what instrument is right for each — a separately read set of real rules, a range drawn from a different comparison group, or an explicit refusal to generate until somebody reads their actual law? And if the range is kept for one of them, what should it be ranged over, given that the thing being interpolated is not the thing the endpoints were measured from?

title: Whether the national range is the right instrument for Puerto Rico and DC
usableAnswer: A position per jurisdiction, for DC and for Puerto Rico separately. For each: whether the national range applies, and if not, whether the answer is to read its real law, to range it against a different comparison group (naming which), or to decline to generate and let the jurisdiction be explicitly unsupported for now. A sentence on legislature structure for each is enough to act on, since the generator mirrors structure.
whyItMatters: This decides whether two of the fifty-two jurisdictions a player can start in are simulated with rules that were inferred from a comparison group they are not members of. The owner's standing rule is that an unresearched jurisdiction gets a realistic range rather than a refusal or an average, and that real law always overrides — but that rule was framed around states. Applying it unexamined to a territory and a federal district produces confident, stable, wrong rules, which is worse than a declared gap because nothing on the surface says the number was interpolated from the wrong population. It is also the difference between a jurisdiction the game can honestly claim to cover and one it merely does not crash in.

answer.summary:
Do not infer D.C. or Puerto Rico's institutional topology from a range of states. Use their own recorded structural profiles with the same shared office/term/authority/legislature machinery; a separate profile is not a separate engine. Reuse the banked D.C. evidence. Puerto Rico scope is already approved, but its factual offices/qualification rows still require the separately queued compilation.

An approved authored game assumption may fill a compatible unresolved parameter inside an accurately identified institution; it cannot manufacture a state governor or a second chamber where there is none. A present-day source-observation timestamp is also not automatically the rule's historical commencement date. Do not let a source-fetch timestamp ban an otherwise approved contemporary game profile. Broader exact PR rules remain unresolved and are not fabricated by this connection answer.
